verdict.reasoning: Patient reports symptoms for “about two to three days” and that they became short of breath while running and now with brisk walking; they also report being “just wheezing a bit and coughing. Just generally a bit short of breath,” indicating exertional worsening.
When asked about phlegm the patient states, “No, I don’t. I’m not coughing up much sputum,” indicating essentially no sputum.
In response to “have you ever been admitted in hospital because your asthma was so bad?” the patient answers, “No, I haven’t.”
To “When was the last time you had an asthma attack?” the patient replies, “About three to four years ago.”

The doctor asks, “you didn’t have any oral steroids or antibiotics?” and the patient says, “Not that I can remember,” which is uncertainty, not a clear report of no prior use. The fact asserts definite absence of both.
Patient says, “I think 130,” then the clinician clarifies, “Okay. Let’s say it’s about 380… so that’s your normal,” agreeing on approximately 380 as baseline peak flow.

The entire consultation is about asthma management; the clinician refers to “because your asthma was so bad” and “when was the last time you had an asthma attack?” implying established asthma diagnosis.
The clinician says, “So you have eczema also?” and later the patient says, “I’ve got a few issues that I think could be eczema as well,” indicating possible eczema.

Patient initially: “I’ve used my blue inhaler, but to no avail,” and later, “salbutamol is just like as and when,” and also, “Yeah, and morning and evening to kind of prevent it as well,” indicating both daily and as-needed use of the blue (salbutamol) inhaler.
When asked, “So how are you using the Klenol? Is it twice a day?” the patient answers, “Yes,” confirming twice-daily Klenil use.
Patient lists current medications: “salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I’m taking as well,” indicating use of cetraben.
In the same list the patient includes “hydrocortisone that I’m taking as well,” indicating use of hydrocortisone.
In response to “Do you have any allergies at all?” the patient answers, “I have hay fever.”
When asked, “any med. Allergies to medication?” the patient replies, “Oh, no, sorry,” and the clinician summarizes, “Okay, so you’re not allergic to anything. Okay, so no allergies.”
Patient states, “My brother’s asthmatic…” indicating a brother with asthma.
The same sentence includes, “…and my sister has eczema,” indicating a sister with eczema.
Combined statement: “My brother’s asthmatic and my sister has eczema” summarizes the family history exactly as described.

Clinician says, “it looks like you can be having a small, small exacerbation,” and the history describes “short of breath,” “wheezing a bit and coughing,” poor response to blue inhaler (“to no avail”), and increased use (“using it every day… morning and evening”), consistent with a mild, subacute asthma exacerbation.
While cetraben and hydrocortisone are mentioned, there is no explicit assessment of eczema status (e.g., “stable”) or direct link that these medications are specifically for eczema management.
Clinician advises, “If you’re using just two puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day” in reference to “the brown inhaler… your clinol.”
The plan includes, “you can use your blue inhaler as and when. Okay. Use it maximum about every two to four hours,” which matches use as needed up to every 2–4 hours.

Clinician states, “I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days… you need a face to face. In the interim… when the doctor sees you, what we’re going to do is… make you do the peak reading,” indicating a face-to-face review for exam and PEFR.

The clinician instructs, “If… you’re using the asthma, you know, the blue inhalers every two to four hours. And your breathing’s getting really worse. Then you would need to take yourself to A. E… if your breathing’s getting worse and you’ve not seen us, do take yourself to A E.”

Reiterated follow-up: “Book an appointment… to see… and I will recommend that you need a face to face… when the doctor sees you, what we’re going to do is… examine your chest… make you do the peak reading,” i.e., urgent face-to-face GP review for exam and PEFR.

The transcript contains no actual examination findings; only future plans: “when the doctor sees you, we’re going to examine your chest.” Therefore stating that no physical examination findings are provided is accurate.

No current peak flow value is measured during this consult; only baseline and future measurement are discussed: “Do you do a peak flow meter at home?” and “when the doctor sees you… make you do the peak reading.” Hence no current PEFR is provided.
